content: Long-term indwelling urinary catheters are frequently used in individuals with lower urinary tract dysfunctions across various settings, including homes, hospitals, and specialized healthcare facilities. However, their use is associated with numerous potential complications and adverse effects. The impact of healthcare policies regarding the replacement of these catheters on patient outcomes remains uncertain. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of different policies for replacing long-term indwelling urinary catheters in adults. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Incontinence Specialised Trials Register, which includes trials from databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, CINAHL, ClinicalTrials.gov, and WHO ICTRP, as well as handsearched journals and conference proceedings. The search was last updated on May 19, 2016. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) investigating policies for replacing long-term urinary catheters in adults were included in the analysis. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were independently performed by at least two review authors. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion or consultation with an independent arbitrator. Authors of the included trials were contacted for clarification when necessary. Three trials met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 107 participants across three healthcare settings: a Veterans Administration nursing home in the USA, a geriatric center in Israel, and a community nursing service in Hong Kong. These trials addressed three specific comparisons: 1. Priefer and colleagues investigated different time intervals for catheter replacement (n = 17). 2. Firestein and colleagues examined the use of antibiotic prophylaxis during catheter replacement (n = 70). 3. Cheung and colleagues compared two types of cleaning solutions for periurethral cleansing (n = 20). All three trials were small in scale and lacked sufficient statistical power. Reporting was inadequate, leading to unclear risk of bias assessments for most domains in two of the three trials. The evidence was insufficient to draw definitive conclusions regarding the following: The incidence of symptomatic urinary tract infections (UTIs) was lower in individuals whose catheters were replaced both monthly and when clinically indicated (risk ratio [RR] 0.35, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.13 to 0.95; very low-quality evidence) compared to those whose catheters were replaced only when clinically indicated. The effect of antibiotic prophylaxis on reducing positive urine cultures at 7 days (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.04), infection rates (RR 1.41, 95% CI 0.55 to 3.65), or mortality (RR 2.12, 95% CI 0.20 to 22.30; very low-quality evidence) could not be adequately assessed. There was no statistically significant difference in the incidence of asymptomatic bacteriuria at 7 days (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.52) between individuals receiving water or chlorhexidine solution for periurethral cleansing during catheter replacement. Notably, none of the 16 participants in this comparison developed symptomatic catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) by day 14. Several critical outcomes for decision-making, such as participant satisfaction, condition-specific quality of life, urinary tract trauma, and formal economic analysis, were not reported in any of the trials. Additionally, no trials compared the following policies: Catheter replacement versus alternative policies (e.g., washouts). Replacement in home versus clinical environments. Clean versus aseptic techniques for catheter replacement. Different lubricants or the absence of lubricant during replacement. Catheter replacement performed by the user, a caregiver, or a healthcare professional. In conclusion, there is currently insufficient evidence to determine the impact of different policies for replacing long-term urinary catheters on patient outcomes. Many policies remain unexamined, and several important outcomes, including patient satisfaction, quality of life, urinary tract trauma, and economic considerations, have not been assessed. There is an urgent need for well-designed, adequately powered randomized controlled trials that evaluate clinically relevant outcomes and adhere to the principles of the CONSORT statement.
